candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on the Gospel of John
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XII.15 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

The threefold question — 'Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these?' — Cyril reads as the deliberate counterpart to Peter's threefold denial. Christ's repetition is restorative, not accusatory: each affirmation of love undoes one denial. 'More than these' (pleon toutōn) Cyril reads as referring to the other disciples (Peter had boasted in 13:37 that he would die for Christ even if all others fell away — Christ now tests the boast). The Greek verbal play (agapē / phileō) Cyril notes but treats with characteristic restraint: both verbs in John often function as synonyms; the deeper distinction is in the questioning-and-answering pattern itself, not in word-choice subtleties.

candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on the Gospel of John
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XII.17 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Feed my sheep' (boske ta probata mou) — the third and culminating commission to Peter — Cyril takes as the dominical institution of the pastoral office. The shift from 'lambs' (arnia, in v. 15) to 'sheep' (probata, in v. 17) Cyril reads as moving from the inexperienced new converts to the mature flock — the entire spectrum of pastoral responsibility is committed to Peter and through him to every subsequent pastor. The repetition Cyril sees as marking the deliberate sacramental-commissioning weight: this is not casual exhortation but solemn appointment. The Tewahedo ordination of bishops and priests preserves this verse's institutional weight in its consecration prayers.

'More than these' (pleon toutōn) Cyril reads as referring to the other disciples (Peter had boasted in 13:37 that he would die for Christ even if all others fell away — Christ now tests the boast). The Greek verbal play (agapē / phileō) Cyril notes but treats with characteristic restraint: both verbs in John often function as synonyms; the deeper distinction is in the questioning-and-answering pattern itself, not in word-choice subtleties.

candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Feed my sheep' (boske ta probata mou) — the third and culminating commission to Peter — Cyril takes as the dominical institution of the pastoral office. The shift from 'lambs' (arnia, in v. 15) to 'sheep' (probata, in v. 17) Cyril reads as moving from the inexperienced new converts to the mature flock — the entire spectrum of pastoral responsibility is committed to Peter and through him to every subsequent pastor. The repetition Cyril sees as marking the deliberate sacramental-commissioning weight: this is not casual exhortation but solemn appointment. The Tewahedo ordination of bishops and priests preserves this verse's institutional weight in its consecration prayers.
